# Prepare a circuit with explicit node IDs

Start with `vignette("getting-started", package = "landconn")` for the distinction
between incidence connectivity and resistance-surface analysis. This guide
constructs a small artificial landscape so that every input is explicit.
Preparation below runs in ordinary R; solver chunks require local Julia and
Circuitscape and are shown without execution during package checking.

```{r prepare, fig.alt="Uniform illustrative habitat with four separated polygon cores carrying explicit IDs."}
library(landconn)
library(terra)
habitat <- rast(nrows = 8, ncols = 8, xmin = 0, xmax = 8, ymin = 0, ymax = 8,
                 crs = "EPSG:3857")
values(habitat) <- 1
points <- vect(cbind(c(1.5, 6.5, 6.5, 1.5), c(1.5, 1.5, 6.5, 6.5)),
                crs = crs(habitat))
points$core_id <- c(44L, 11L, 33L, 22L)
cores <- buffer(points, width = 0.6)
plot(habitat)
plot(cores, add = TRUE)
```

Rows deliberately have unsorted IDs. `field = "core_id"` preserves these values;
the returned pairwise matrix is labeled by ID. Without a field, row numbers
become IDs. Every core must cover at least one valid habitat cell. Very small
polygons or overlapping cores may disappear when rasterized and produce a clear
error. Point features must occupy distinct cells.

Habitat values must be positive and finite. Mark excluded cells with `NA`, not a
large resistance code. All grids use the same extent, square cell size and
coordinate system. Missing cells outside focal nodes are serialized as nodata;
they never become an additional core. Coordinates with undeclared CRS are assumed
aligned, so supplying a correct shared CRS is preferable.

# Set up Julia once

```{r julia, eval=FALSE}
jl_home <- "C:/path/to/Julia/bin" # replace with your installation directory
julia_packages(jl_home, install_libraries = TRUE)
```

Installation changes the active Julia package environment and needs network
access. Only Circuitscape is installed; ConScape and plotting libraries are not
required by this workflow. On subsequent sessions, use
`install_libraries = FALSE`. For reproducible projects, retain a Julia project
and its package versions. Local integration was verified with Julia 1.12.6 and
Circuitscape 5.17.1. The optional CI job pins that Circuitscape version; other
versions require their own integration validation.

# Pairwise resistance and output maps

```{r pairwise, eval=FALSE}
distances <- run_cs(jl_home, habitat, cores, field = "core_id",
                     output = "matrix", CurrentMap = FALSE)
distances

maps <- run_cs(jl_home, habitat, cores, field = "core_id",
                output_dir = tempdir(), output_name = "core_demo",
                cumulative_map_only = FALSE, VoltageMaps = TRUE)
plot(maps[[1]])
```

**How to read the matrix:** rows and columns are circuit node IDs, rather than
the original feature row order. Entries are effective resistance under the
specified landscape and connection rule. The diagonal is zero. Larger values
indicate greater electrical isolation in this modeled circuit; they are not
geographic distances or calibrated dispersal probabilities.

**How to read the maps:** the first layer is cumulative current. Requested
individual pair currents follow, then voltages. File stems identify layers.
Projection sidecars are excluded when loading maps. Current concentrates along
routes favored by this resistance and node design. That makes high-current cells
candidates for closer assessment, rather than proving the effect of habitat loss.
SpatRaster inputs return a SpatRaster; legacy RasterLayer inputs return a legacy
Raster object. Maximum-current maps, when requested, are saved separately.

To select pairs, order node IDs increasingly, then use the column-wise lower
triangle. For IDs 11, 22, 33, 44, the order is (22,11), (33,11), (44,11),
(33,22), (44,22), (44,33).

```{r pairs, eval=FALSE}
selected <- run_cs(jl_home, habitat, cores, field = "core_id",
                    output = "matrix", CurrentMap = FALSE,
                    pairs_to_include = c(1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0))
```

Only selected pairs are solved. Inspect the returned node labels: IDs absent
from all retained pairs may be omitted by Circuitscape. At least one pair must be
retained. Pair selection is rejected in scenarios without this contract.

# Per-node strengths and advanced grounds

```{r per-node, eval=FALSE}
strengths <- cbind(node_id = c(11, 22, 33, 44), amperes = c(1, 2, 1, 1))
nodes <- run_cs(jl_home, habitat, cores, field = "core_id", scenario = "one-to-all",
                 variable_source = strengths, CurrentMap = FALSE, output = "matrix")
nodes
```

One-to-all and all-to-one return a two-column matrix, `node_id` and `resistance`,
with every focal ID retained. Unlike pairwise output, there is no header row to
remove. Strengths are a two-column ID/amperes table; IDs not listed keep the
solver's default unit strength. Values reported by these scenarios should be
interpreted with their source and ground design, especially when strengths differ.

Advanced mode instead attaches sources and grounds to the listed core IDs:

```{r advanced, eval=FALSE}
voltage <- run_cs(jl_home, habitat, cores, field = "core_id", scenario = "advanced",
                   variable_source = cbind(11, 1),  # one ampere at core 11
                   variable_ground = cbind(44, 0),  # direct ground at core 44
                   CurrentMap = FALSE, output = "matrix")
```

The returned matrix is a complete voltage grid in raster row/column order,
without any stripped rows. For each polygon core, one source or ground is
attached to its first represented cell; all cells with that region ID are
collapsed into a single circuit node. Thus the source is a total current per
core, not a repeated injection into every cell. Ground values are resistances
to ground, with zero denoting a direct ground, even for conductance habitat.
Source and ground IDs must be disjoint. A point ID occupying multiple cells is
rejected in advanced mode because it is not a single short-circuited node.

Supplying `regions = cores` selects one valid raster cell per region as the
focal node, replacing any supplied point locations. Sampling preserves each
region ID and excludes habitat nodata cells. Set a seed before the call to
reproduce the selection.

# Omnidirectional maps and masks

```{r omni, eval=FALSE}
habitat[28] <- NA # an excluded internal cell remains excluded during the solve
set.seed(100)
omni <- omni_cs(jl_home, habitat, n_nodes = 12)
plot(omni)
```

This adapts the perimeter-node idea in Koen et al. (2014). Their study used
random perimeter nodes and pairwise connections. This implementation uses
regularly spaced unique perimeter cells and all-to-one solves, so the two designs
should not be assumed equivalent. Each node is grounded in turn while the
remaining nodes supply current.

The buffer extends by 25% of the original row/column counts on each side,
rounded down with at least one added row and column. Only new buffer cells
receive positive values drawn as the absolute value of a normal distribution
with mean 5 and standard deviation 1. Original missing cells remain excluded
throughout the solve and in the cropped output. Exactly `n_nodes` distinct cells
are used; requesting more nodes than the perimeter can hold is an error. Repeat
the analysis with different seeds to assess sensitivity to this artificial buffer.

# Threads, errors and retained files

For parallel work, set threads before Julia starts. A running process cannot
change its Julia thread count. In a fresh R session:

```{r threads, eval=FALSE}
distances <- run_cs(jl_home, habitat, cores, field = "core_id",
                     parallel = TRUE, cores = 2, output = "matrix",
                     CurrentMap = FALSE)
```

The actual Julia thread count is checked. A mismatch is an actionable error,
not a silently ignored core count. R environment variables are restored after
the call; the Julia process itself persists. Parallel execution does not promise
a speed improvement for a small grid.

Temporary input grids and configurations are cleaned on success and failure by
default. `remove_files = FALSE` retains them for investigation. Requested solver
output maps remain in `output_dir`. Use a distinct output name for each run.
Errors retain the original solver message, and configuration writing preserves
the caller's output redirection.

# Quick reference

```{r quick, eval=FALSE}
distances <- run_cs(jl_home, habitat, cores, field = "core_id",
                     output = "matrix", CurrentMap = FALSE) # named resistance matrix
maps <- run_cs(jl_home, habitat, cores, field = "core_id")   # cumulative current first
set.seed(100)
omni <- omni_cs(jl_home, habitat, n_nodes = 12)              # original mask retained
```

| Function | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
| `julia_packages()` | Optionally install and load Circuitscape |
| `run_cs()` | Prepare ID grids and run a specified circuit design |
| `omni_cs()` | Accumulate current under a buffered perimeter-node design |

See `vignette("getting-started", package = "landconn")` and
`vignette("model-engines", package = "landconn")` for the incidence workflows.

connectivity for wildlife: development and validation of multispecies linkage
maps. *Methods in Ecology and Evolution*, 5(7), 626-633.
